questions.stem: Which statement describes DNA in a eukaryotic cell nucleus?
options: It is made of ribose nucleotides joined into a single helix
It is bound to histone proteins in linear chromosomes
It is unbound and circular, lying free in the cytosol
It is single-stranded and bound to ribosomes in the nucleus
questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, DNA is wound around histone proteins and packaged into linear chromosomes inside the nucleus. Unbound circular DNA is found in prokaryotes and in mitochondria and chloroplasts.

questions.stem: Which comparison of chromosomes in prokaryotes and eukaryotes is correct?
options: Prokaryotes: several linear chromosomes in a nucleus; eukaryotes: one circular one
Prokaryotes: DNA inside mitochondria only; eukaryotes: DNA inside ribosomes only
Prokaryotes: circular DNA not bound to histones; eukaryotes: linear DNA on histones
Prokaryotes: linear DNA on histones; eukaryotes: circular DNA in the cytosol
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes usually have a single circular chromosome in the cytosol, not bound to histones. Eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes, with DNA bound to histones, inside a nucleus.

questions.stem: Mitochondria contain their own DNA. What form does this DNA take?
options: Single-stranded RNA, like the genome of a virus
Short linear fragments joined to the ribosomes
Circular and unbound, like prokaryotic DNA
Linear and bound to histones, like nuclear DNA
questions.explanation: DNA in mitochondria and chloroplasts is circular and not bound to histones, resembling prokaryotic DNA. This is one line of evidence that these organelles descended from prokaryotes.

questions.stem: Which list gives the parts of one nucleotide in a DNA strand?
options: Ribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
Deoxyribose, an amino acid and a phosphate group
Glucose, a phosphate group and a long fatty acid chain
Deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: A DNA nucleotide consists of the sugar deoxyribose, a phosphate group and one of four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine or guanine. Ribose is found in RNA nucleotides.

questions.stem: Why is it important that the two strands of DNA are held together by weak hydrogen bonds between bases?
options: The strands can never separate, so the genetic information stays fully protected
Weak bonds allow the bases to swap partners freely, so that A can then pair with C instead
Weak bonds let the sugar-phosphate backbone dissolve and reform at each division
The strands can separate for replication and transcription without breaking the backbone
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are weak enough to be broken by enzymes, letting the strands unzip for replication and transcription, while the strong covalent bonds of the sugar-phosphate backbone stay intact. Base pairing remains A with T and C with G.

questions.stem: A DNA sample contains 22% adenine. What percentage of its bases are guanine?
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs with thymine, so thymine is also 22%, making 44% A + T. The remaining 56% is shared equally between guanine and cytosine, so guanine is 28%.

questions.stem: One strand of DNA has the sequence 5' ATGCCTAG 3'. What is the sequence of its complementary strand, written 3' to 5'?
options: 3' TACGGATC 5'
3' ATGCCTAG 5'
3' UACGGAUC 5'
3' GATCCGTA 5'
questions.explanation: Each base pairs with its complement: A with T and C with G, so ATGCCTAG pairs with TACGGATC, running in the opposite direction. U appears only in RNA, not DNA.

questions.stem: What does 'semi-conservative' mean in DNA replication?
options: Each new DNA molecule has one original strand and one new strand
One new DNA molecule has both original strands, the other has two new strands
Each new DNA molecule is made of short pieces of old and new DNA mixed at random
Half of the genes in the original molecule are copied and the rest are lost
questions.explanation: In semi-conservative replication, the two strands separate and each acts as a template for a new complementary strand. Each daughter molecule therefore conserves one original strand.

questions.stem: Bacteria grown for many generations on heavy nitrogen (15N) are moved to normal nitrogen (14N) and allowed to replicate their DNA twice. What proportion of the DNA molecules then contain a heavy strand?
options: One quarter
All of them
Three quarters
One half
questions.explanation: After the first replication, both molecules are hybrid (one heavy, one light strand). In the second, each hybrid gives one hybrid and one fully light molecule, so 2 of the 4 molecules (one half) contain a heavy strand.

questions.stem: Why are the base-pairing rules and the method of DNA replication described as universal?
options: They differ in each species, but give the same final result
They are the same in all living things, reflecting common ancestry
They are the same in all eukaryotes but different in all prokaryotes
They were invented by scientists and applied to every organism
questions.explanation: All organisms store information in DNA with the same base pairing, A with T and C with G, and copy it by the same semi-conservative method. This shared system is evidence that all life descends from a common ancestor.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic gene, what are introns?
options: Non-coding segments that are transcribed but removed before translation
Coding segments that are translated directly into the polypeptide
Segments that are removed from the DNA before transcription begins
Segments of mRNA added to the ends to protect the molecule from breaking down
questions.explanation: Both exons and introns are transcribed into the initial RNA. The introns are then removed and the exons joined, so only the information in exons is translated into the polypeptide.

questions.stem: A eukaryotic gene is 12 000 nucleotides long, but the mature mRNA from it is only 3000 nucleotides long. What is the best explanation?
options: Introns were transcribed and then removed from the RNA before translation
Exons were removed from the DNA before the gene could be transcribed
Only one of the four bases in the gene was copied into the mRNA molecule
The ribosome cut the mRNA into four equal pieces and then used only one of them
questions.explanation: The whole gene, exons and introns, is transcribed, and then the introns are cut out and the exons joined. A mature mRNA much shorter than the gene indicates that much of the gene consists of introns.

questions.stem: Which molecules can be the end products of genes?
options: Only functional proteins such as enzymes and hormones
Only mRNA, which is the final product of every gene
Glucose, lipids and other energy-storage molecules
Functional proteins, tRNA, rRNA and microRNA
questions.explanation: A gene codes for either a functional protein or a functional RNA molecule. Genes for tRNA, rRNA and microRNA are transcribed but not translated; their RNA is the final product.

questions.stem: In a eukaryotic cell, where does transcription occur?
options: In the nucleus
At the ribosomes
In the Golgi body
In the cytoskeleton
questions.explanation: Transcription, the making of an RNA copy of a gene, takes place in the nucleus where the DNA is. The mRNA then moves to the ribosomes in the cytoplasm for translation.

questions.stem: What is the role of transfer RNA (tRNA) in protein synthesis?
options: It forms the main structure of the ribosome together with proteins
It joins the exons back together after all of the introns have been removed
It carries a specific amino acid and pairs its anticodon with an mRNA codon
It carries the code for the protein from the nucleus to the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Each tRNA carries one particular amino acid and has an anticodon complementary to an mRNA codon, so amino acids are placed in the order the mRNA specifies. mRNA carries the code from the nucleus, and rRNA forms part of the ribosome.

questions.stem: The template strand of a gene contains the triplet 3' TAC 5'. What is the mRNA codon, and what is the tRNA anticodon that pairs with it?
options: mRNA codon AUG; anticodon UAC
mRNA codon TAC; anticodon AUG
mRNA codon UAC; anticodon AUG
mRNA codon ATG; anticodon TAC
questions.explanation: mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with U in place of T, so TAC gives AUG. The tRNA anticodon is complementary to the codon, giving UAC. DNA bases such as T never appear in RNA.

questions.stem: The coding strand of a short gene reads 5' ATG TTC GGA 3'. What is the sequence of the mRNA made from this gene?
options: 5' AUG UUC GGA 3'
5' UAC AAG CCU 3'
5' TAC AAG CCT 3'
3' AUG UUC GGA 5'
questions.explanation: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, so it has the same sequence and direction as the coding strand, with U replacing T. Writing the complement of the coding strand gives the template-strand pattern, not the mRNA.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the coding strand from the template strand of a gene?
options: The coding strand is read during transcription; the template strand matches the mRNA
The coding strand is found only in prokaryotes; the template strand only in eukaryotes
Both strands are read at once, giving two different mRNA molecules for each gene
The template strand is read during transcription; the coding strand matches the mRNA
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template strand and builds an mRNA complementary to it. The mRNA therefore has the same base sequence as the coding (gene) strand, apart from U replacing T.

questions.stem: By convention, in which direction are DNA sequences written and read?
options: Left to right on the template only
From the centromere outwards
questions.explanation: DNA strands are directional, with a 5' end and a 3' end. By convention, sequences are written 5' to 3', and RNA polymerase builds mRNA in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.stem: Part of an mRNA reads 5' AUG GCU UGG 3'. Using AUG = methionine, GCU = alanine and UGG = tryptophan, what is the amino acid sequence, and how many tRNA molecules deliver it?
options: Methionine-alanine-tryptophan, delivered by three tRNAs
Tryptophan-alanine-methionine, delivered by three tRNAs
Methionine-alanine-tryptophan, delivered by nine tRNAs
Methionine-alanine-tryptophan, delivered by one tRNA
questions.explanation: The ribosome reads codons 5' to 3', one triplet at a time, so the order is methionine, alanine, tryptophan. Each codon is matched by one tRNA anticodon, so three tRNAs deliver three amino acids, not one per base.

questions.stem: What determines the primary structure of a protein?
options: The number of separate polypeptide chains that are combined
The folding of its chain into a three-dimensional shape
The sequence of amino acids in its polypeptide chain
The coiling of its chain into helices and pleated sheets
questions.explanation: Primary structure is the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, as coded by the gene. It determines how the chain folds into its secondary and tertiary structures.

questions.stem: Which type of bond holds the alpha helices and beta pleated sheets of a protein's secondary structure in shape?
options: Peptide bonds
Disulfide bridges only
Phosphodiester bonds
Hydrogen bonds
questions.explanation: Secondary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds between parts of the polypeptide backbone. Peptide bonds join amino acids in the primary structure, and disulfide bridges help hold tertiary structure.

questions.stem: Haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains joined together. Which level of protein structure does this describe?
options: Quaternary
Tertiary
Secondary
Primary
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the association of two or more polypeptide chains into one functional protein, as in haemoglobin. Tertiary structure is the three-dimensional folding of a single chain.

questions.stem: A mutation replaces one amino acid in an enzyme with another that cannot form a disulfide bridge. Why might the enzyme stop working even though only one amino acid changed?
options: The primary structure stays the same, so the enzyme loses all its bonds
The enzyme gains an extra polypeptide chain and blocks its active site
The change makes the enzyme bind every substrate in the cell at once
The tertiary folding changes, altering the shape of the active site
questions.explanation: A change in primary structure can alter the bonds that hold the tertiary structure, such as a disulfide bridge, so the three-dimensional shape and the active site change. Function depends on shape, so the substrate may no longer fit.

questions.stem: Why is the three-dimensional shape of a receptor protein critical to its function?
options: Its binding site must be complementary to its specific signal molecule
Its shape decides how many genes the cell carries in the DNA of its nucleus
Its shape allows it to bind any molecule that touches the cell
Its shape provides energy for transporting molecules into the cell
questions.explanation: Proteins such as enzymes, receptors, some hormones and antibodies work by binding specific molecules, which requires a complementary shape. If the shape changes, the specific molecule can no longer bind.

questions.stem: How do enzymes increase the rate of a reaction?
options: By being used up as one of the reactants
By lowering the activation energy needed
By raising the temperature of the cell
By supplying the energy the products store
questions.explanation: Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy, so more molecules have enough energy to react at body temperature. They are not used up and do not change the overall energy of the reaction.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the induced-fit model of enzyme action?
options: The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, giving a close fit
The active site is rigid and fits the substrate exactly like a key in a lock
The substrate changes the enzyme's primary structure each time it binds
The enzyme binds to any substrate and then changes its shape to suit each one in turn
questions.explanation: In the induced-fit model, the active site is flexible and moulds itself around the specific substrate as it binds, straining bonds and lowering activation energy. A rigid active site is the older lock-and-key model.

questions.stem: An enzyme's activity is measured from 10 °C to 60 °C. Activity rises to a peak at 37 °C, then falls to zero by 55 °C. Cooling the 55 °C sample back to 37 °C does not restore activity. Why?
options: Low temperature at the start used up all of the substrate in the sample
The enzyme became inactive at 55 °C only because molecules moved too slowly
Cooling the enzyme removed its activation energy, so it can no longer react
High temperature denatured the enzyme, permanently changing its active site
questions.explanation: Above the optimum, increased vibration breaks the bonds holding the tertiary structure, so the active site loses its shape. This denaturation is generally permanent, unlike the reversible slowing of activity at low temperature.

questions.stem: A drug molecule has a shape similar to an enzyme's substrate and binds to the active site without reacting. What effect does it have?
options: It acts as an inhibitor, reducing the rate by blocking substrate binding
It acts as a substrate, increasing the amount of product formed
It acts as a catalyst, lowering the activation energy further
It acts as a cofactor, helping the substrate fit more closely into the active site
questions.explanation: A molecule that occupies the active site without reacting is a competitive inhibitor, preventing substrate molecules from binding and slowing the reaction. Drugs such as ritonavir work by inhibiting a specific enzyme.

questions.stem: With enzyme concentration fixed, increasing substrate concentration raises the reaction rate at first, but then the rate levels off. What limits the rate at high substrate concentration?
options: The substrate has denatured the enzyme, so fewer active sites remain
The product has been used up, so no more reactions can take place
The activation energy has risen, so fewer of the substrate molecules are able to react
All active sites are occupied, so enzyme concentration becomes limiting
questions.explanation: At high substrate concentrations, every active site is occupied at any moment, so adding more substrate cannot speed the reaction. Adding more enzyme would raise the rate further.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes transcription factors?
options: Enzymes that join amino acids together at the ribosome during translation
Sections of RNA that are removed before translation begins
Nucleotides that are added to the end of a new DNA strand
Proteins that bind DNA and switch transcription of genes on or off
questions.explanation: Transcription factors are proteins, themselves the products of other genes, that bind to DNA near a gene and promote or block its transcription. They allow different genes to be expressed in different cells and conditions.

questions.stem: How does DNA methylation usually affect a gene?
options: It doubles the number of copies of the gene in the cell
It increases transcription by unwinding the DNA from histones
It silences the gene by reducing its transcription
It changes the base sequence of the gene permanently
questions.explanation: Adding methyl groups to DNA, often near the start of a gene, usually reduces or prevents transcription. It changes gene expression without changing the DNA base sequence, which is why it is called an epigenetic change.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same DNA sequence, yet by age 50 they often differ in their risk of certain diseases. Which explanation is best supported by epigenetics?
options: One twin inherited extra chromosomes from their parents after birth
Identical twins never have the same DNA, so they always differ in disease risk
Different environments altered methylation and histone marks, changing gene expression
Each twin's DNA base sequence changed in every cell to suit their environment
questions.explanation: Over time, factors such as diet, smoking and stress can change DNA methylation and histone modification differently in each twin. This alters gene expression, and so phenotype, without changing the DNA sequence.

questions.stem: In some cancers, the region at the start of a gene that normally stops cell division becomes heavily methylated. Why can this lead to a tumour?
options: The gene is copied many times over, so the cells divide much more slowly than normal
The methyl groups change the gene's base sequence into a different gene
The extra methylation makes the cells undergo meiosis instead of mitosis
The gene is silenced, so cells lose a brake on division and divide uncontrollably
questions.explanation: Methylation silences the gene that normally restrains cell division, so its protein is not made. Without this control, cells can divide uncontrollably and form a tumour, even though the DNA sequence is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which factor increases the rate of mutation?
options: Eating food that contains protein
Normal body temperature of 37 °C
Ionising radiation such as X-rays
Drinking water at room temperature
questions.explanation: Mutation rates are increased by mutagens: ionising radiation, mutagenic chemicals such as some in tobacco smoke, and some viruses. Mutations can also arise from errors in DNA replication or cell division.

questions.stem: Using UUU = phenylalanine, UUC = phenylalanine and UUA = leucine, what is the effect of a point mutation that changes an mRNA codon from UUU to UUC?
options: Every amino acid after this codon is changed because the reading frame shifts along
No change in the amino acid, because both codons code for phenylalanine
Phenylalanine is replaced by leucine, changing the protein's sequence
Translation stops early, so the protein is much shorter than normal
questions.explanation: UUU and UUC both code for phenylalanine, so this substitution is silent and the protein is unchanged. A substitution does not change the reading frame, unlike an insertion or deletion.

questions.stem: Why does deleting one nucleotide near the start of a gene usually affect the protein much more than substituting one nucleotide?
options: The deletion changes only one codon, while substitution changes all of them
The deletion removes the whole gene from the chromosome in each cell
The deletion turns the DNA into RNA, so it cannot be transcribed
The deletion shifts the reading frame, changing every codon after it
questions.explanation: Codons are read in groups of three, so deleting a single base shifts the reading frame and alters every codon downstream, often producing a non-functional protein or an early stop. A substitution affects at most one codon.

questions.stem: A mutation occurs in a skin cell of an adult exposed to ultraviolet light. Why will it not be passed on to the person's children?
options: It is a germline mutation, so it is removed during fertilisation
All mutations caused by ultraviolet light are repaired before birth
Skin cells contain no DNA at all, so the mutation cannot be inherited by children
It is a somatic mutation, not present in the cells that make gametes
questions.explanation: Mutations in somatic (body) cells affect only that person, and may cause problems such as skin cancer. Only germline mutations, in cells that produce eggs or sperm, can be inherited by offspring.

questions.stem: A germline mutation produces a new allele in a population of mice. Which outcome can follow over many generations?
options: The allele is always harmful, so it is removed from the population in the first generation
The allele can be inherited, changing the characteristics of some descendants
The allele affects only the mouse in which it arose and is lost at its death
The allele changes every cell of all mice in the population at the same time
questions.explanation: Germline mutations are in gametes, so they can be passed to offspring and spread through descendants, changing their characteristics. Whether the allele becomes common depends on its effect and on chance; not all mutations are harmful.

questions.stem: Which is a chromosomal mutation rather than a point mutation?
options: One base in a gene is replaced by a different base during replication
One base is inserted into a codon, shifting the reading frame of a gene
One codon is changed to a stop codon by a single base substitution
A section of a chromosome is broken off and attached to another chromosome
questions.explanation: Chromosomal mutations affect large parts of chromosomes or whole chromosomes, as in translocation, deletion or duplication of a segment. Changes to single bases, including frameshifts, are gene mutations.
